11-01.script:
The first of November begins with candles. Across much of the world it is All Saints' Day, and in Mexico families build bright altars for the Day of the Dead, welcoming back the memories of those they love.

On this day in 1512, the doors of the Sistine Chapel opened to reveal Michelangelo's ceiling, four years of painting high on a scaffold, with God reaching out to Adam across the sky.

But in 1755, the morning of All Saints' Day brought terror to Lisbon. A great earthquake, then a tsunami and fires, swept through one of Europe's grandest cities.

In 1800, John Adams moved into an unfinished house in Washington and became the first president to live in the White House. In his first letter there, he prayed that only honest and wise men would ever rule under its roof.

In India, Karnataka and Kerala celebrate the days their states were formed. A day of light, of memory, and of home.

11-02.script:
On the second of November, families in Mexico gather in candlelit cemeteries, decorated with marigolds, to share food and stories with those who have passed. It is the Day of the Dead, and for many Christians, All Souls' Day.

On this day in 1920, a radio station in Pittsburgh called KDKA broadcast the results of the American presidential election. It was the start of commercial radio, and soon voices would travel into every home.

Sixteen years later, in 1936, the BBC began the world's first regular high-definition television service from Alexandra Palace in London.

In 1947, Howard Hughes took the controls of a giant wooden flying boat, nicknamed the Spruce Goose. It lifted off the water for less than a minute, and never flew again.

And in 2000, three astronauts floated into the International Space Station. Ever since that day, there has always been someone living in space.

Born on this day in 1965 was Shah Rukh Khan, who would become one of the most beloved film stars in the world.

11-03.script:
On the third of November in 1957, a small dog named Laika was strapped into Sputnik 2 and launched into orbit. She became the first animal to circle the Earth, and she never came home. She is still remembered as one of the first explorers of space.

In 1973, NASA launched Mariner 10 towards Venus and Mercury, the first spacecraft to use the pull of one planet to fling itself towards another.

In 1903, Panama separated from Colombia, and soon a great canal would be cut across its narrow land. Today Panama celebrates its independence.

In 1954, a giant creature rose from the sea in a Japanese film. Godzilla was born, a monster made from the fears of the atomic age.

And in Japan, today is Culture Day, a celebration of art, learning and peace. Born on this day in 1933 was Amartya Sen, the economist who taught the world that development means giving people the freedom to live the lives they value.

11-04.script:
On the fourth of November in 1922, in the Valley of the Kings in Egypt, a water boy is said to have uncovered a stone step in the sand. Howard Carter's team dug further, and found a staircase leading down to a sealed door. Behind it lay the tomb of the boy king Tutankhamun, untouched for more than three thousand years.

The fourth of November has also seen hard days. In 1979, students in Tehran seized the American embassy, beginning a hostage crisis that lasted 444 days. In 1995, Israel's Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin, who had worked for peace, was assassinated at a rally in Tel Aviv.

But in 2008, crowds gathered in Chicago's Grant Park to celebrate as Barack Obama was elected the first African American president of the United States.

Today Russia celebrates National Unity Day. And born on this day in 1916 was Walter Cronkite, the newsman once called the most trusted man in America.

11-05.script:
Remember, remember, the fifth of November. In 1605, guards searching the cellars beneath the Houses of Parliament found a man named Guy Fawkes standing beside barrels of gunpowder. The Gunpowder Plot to blow up King James was foiled, and Britain still lights bonfires and fireworks on this night.

Centuries later, in 1872, Susan B. Anthony walked into a polling station in Rochester, New York, and cast a vote, even though women were not allowed to. Two weeks later she was arrested, but her cause would win in the end.

In 2013, India launched a small orbiter called Mangalyaan towards Mars. It reached the red planet on its very first attempt, at a cost less than many Hollywood films.

Today is also World Tsunami Awareness Day.

And born on this day in 1988 was Virat Kohli, one of the greatest batsmen of his generation.

11-06.script:
On the sixth of November in 1869, two college teams, Rutgers and Princeton, met on a field in New Jersey to play a rough new game with a round ball. It was the first intercollegiate football game in America.

In 1860, Abraham Lincoln was elected president. Within weeks, southern states began to leave the Union, and the nation moved towards civil war.

In 1913, in South Africa, Mahatma Gandhi led thousands of Indian miners on a peaceful march against unjust laws, and was arrested. It was one of the first great tests of non-violent resistance.

In 1917, after months of rain and mud, Canadian troops captured the village of Passchendaele, ending one of the most terrible battles of the First World War.

Born on this day in 1814 was Adolphe Sax, a Belgian instrument maker. He invented the saxophone, and the world of music was never quite the same.

11-07.script:
Born on the seventh of November in 1867, in Warsaw, was a girl named Maria Skłodowska. As Marie Curie, she would discover radium and polonium, and become the first person to win two Nobel Prizes. Today, India marks National Cancer Awareness Day on her birthday, honouring the science she began.

Also born on this day, in 1888, was C. V. Raman, who discovered how light changes colour as it scatters, and won India's first Nobel Prize in science.

In 1917, in Petrograd, the Bolsheviks stormed the Winter Palace. The October Revolution had begun, and Russia would be transformed.

In 1940, high winds set the new Tacoma Narrows Bridge swaying and twisting like a ribbon until it tore apart. Engineers have studied that film ever since.

And in 1990, Mary Robinson was elected the first woman president of Ireland. A day of brilliant minds and bold firsts.

11-08.script:
On the evening of the eighth of November in 1895, in his laboratory in Würzburg, Wilhelm Röntgen noticed a strange glow across the room. Invisible rays were passing through paper, through wood, and even through his own hand. He called them X-rays, and a few weeks later he took a picture of the bones in his wife's hand. Medicine would never be the same.

On this day in 1519, the Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés entered the great Aztec city of Tenochtitlan and met the emperor Moctezuma.

In 1923, in a Munich beer hall, a young Adolf Hitler tried to seize power. The Beer Hall Putsch failed, but it was a warning of darker days.

And in 1960, John F. Kennedy was elected president, the youngest man ever voted into the office.

Born on this day were Edmond Halley in 1656, the astronomer who predicted the return of his famous comet, and Bram Stoker in 1847, who gave the world Dracula.

11-09.script:
On the night of the ninth of November in 1989, an East German official made a confused announcement on television: the borders were open, effective immediately. Crowds rushed to the Berlin Wall. The guards stepped aside, and people climbed onto the Wall, singing and crying, and began to break it apart with hammers. A city divided for twenty-eight years became one again.

The same date carries darker memories in Germany. In 1938, on Kristallnacht, synagogues, shops and homes of Jewish families were attacked across the country. And in 1918, Kaiser Wilhelm the Second gave up his throne.

In 1967, the enormous Saturn V rocket flew for the first time on Apollo 4, and the road to the Moon was open.

Born on this day in 1877 was the poet Muhammad Iqbal, and in 1934, Carl Sagan, who helped millions of people fall in love with the cosmos. He reminded us that we are made of star stuff.

names: World Science Day for Peace and Development
11-10.script:
On the tenth of November in 1871, on the shores of Lake Tanganyika, the journalist Henry Morton Stanley finally found the missing explorer David Livingstone. He raised his hat and, according to his own account, said: Dr. Livingstone, I presume?

On this day in 1969, a new kind of children's show began on American television, with puppets, songs, and a sunny street where everyone was welcome. Sesame Street taught generations of children to count and to read.

In 1975, a great ore ship called the Edmund Fitzgerald sank in a storm on Lake Superior, and its crew was lost. A famous song still keeps their memory alive.

And in 1983, Microsoft announced a new program for its computers, with windows that could open on the screen.

Today is World Science Day for Peace and Development. Born on this day in 1483 was Martin Luther, whose questions would one day change Europe.

11-11.script:
At the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month of 1918, the guns of the First World War fell silent. After four years and millions of lives, soldiers climbed out of the trenches into an unfamiliar quiet. Today, many countries pause for two minutes of silence, and wear red poppies in remembrance.

That same day, Poland regained its independence after more than a century, and Poles celebrate it still.

Long before, in 1620, aboard the Mayflower, anchored off the coast of New England, the passengers signed a short agreement to govern themselves fairly. The Mayflower Compact became a seed of democracy.

In 1572, the astronomer Tycho Brahe looked up and saw a brilliant new star in Cassiopeia. It showed that the heavens were not as unchanging as people believed.

In India, today is National Education Day, the birthday of Maulana Abul Kalam Azad, the country's first education minister. Born on this day too was Fyodor Dostoevsky, in 1821.

A day of silence, and of gratitude.

11-12.script:
On the twelfth of November in 1912, a search party crossing the Antarctic ice found a snow-covered tent. Inside lay Captain Robert Falcon Scott and two companions, who had reached the South Pole and died on the long march home. Beside them were Scott's diaries, still telling their story of courage.

In 1954, the gates of Ellis Island closed. For more than sixty years, millions of immigrants had passed through its halls on their way to new lives in America.

In 1980, Voyager 1 swept past Saturn and sent home pictures of its rings in astonishing detail. And in 2014, after a ten-year journey, a little lander named Philae touched down on a comet for the very first time, bouncing gently across its surface.

Born on this day in 1840 was Auguste Rodin, the sculptor of The Thinker, and in 1961, Nadia Comăneci, who would score the first perfect ten in Olympic gymnastics.

11-13.script:
Today is World Kindness Day, and the thirteenth of November carries stories that remind us why kindness matters.

In 1982, in Washington, a long wall of black granite was dedicated to the Americans who died in Vietnam. Visitors still touch the names carved into the stone, and leave flowers, letters and photographs.

In 1956, the United States Supreme Court ruled that segregated buses in Montgomery, Alabama, were unconstitutional. The bus boycott that had begun with Rosa Parks had won.

In 1985, the volcano Nevado del Ruiz erupted in Colombia, and mudflows buried the town of Armero. The world watched with sorrow, and learned hard lessons about listening to warnings.

And in 2009, scientists announced that a probe crashing into the Moon had found water there, hidden in the shadows of a crater.

Born on this day in 1850 was Robert Louis Stevenson, who wrote Treasure Island, and dreamed of adventures for all of us.

11-14.script:
In India, today is Children's Day, the birthday of Jawaharlal Nehru, the first Prime Minister, who loved spending time with children and was fondly called Chacha Nehru.

On the fourteenth of November in 1889, a young reporter named Nellie Bly set off from New York to travel around the world faster than the hero of a famous novel. She did it in just seventy-two days.

In 1851, a long novel about a white whale was published in America. Moby-Dick was little read at first, and is now one of the great books of all time.

In 1960, a six-year-old girl named Ruby Bridges walked into an all-white school in New Orleans, escorted by federal marshals. Her courage became a symbol of the civil rights movement.

In 1969, Apollo 12 was struck by lightning just after lift-off, but the crew carried on, and landed on the Moon five days later.

Born on this day in 1840 was Claude Monet, who painted light itself.

11-15.script:
On the fifteenth of November in 1875, in the forests of present-day Jharkhand, a boy named Birsa Munda was born. He grew up to lead his people against injustice, and India now honours him today as Janjatiya Gaurav Divas, a day of pride for its tribal communities. The state of Jharkhand was formed on his birthday in 2000.

In 1889, Brazil's emperor was sent into exile, and the country became a republic.

In 1920, representatives of forty-one nations gathered in Geneva for the first assembly of the League of Nations, hoping to prevent another world war.

In 1971, a company called Intel introduced the 4004, a whole computer processor on a single tiny chip. Every smartphone today is its descendant.

And in 2022, the United Nations estimated that the world's population had reached eight billion people.

Born on this day in 1738 was William Herschel, the musician turned astronomer who discovered the planet Uranus.

11-16.script:
Today is the International Day for Tolerance, and India's National Press Day, a celebration of a free and responsible press.

On the sixteenth of November in 1974, astronomers at the great Arecibo telescope in Puerto Rico beamed a short message out into space, aimed at a distant cluster of stars. It carried simple pictures: numbers, a human figure, our solar system. It will take twenty-five thousand years to arrive.

Nearly fifty years later, in 2022, NASA's giant new rocket lifted off on the Artemis One mission and sent an empty capsule around the Moon, the first step towards taking people back.

On Broadway in 1959, the curtain rose on The Sound of Music, and the hills came alive with song.

In 1849, a young writer named Fyodor Dostoevsky was sentenced to death in St. Petersburg. At the last moment, standing before the firing squad, he was spared. He went on to write some of the greatest novels ever written.

11-17.script:
On the seventeenth of November in 1869, a long line of ships sailed into a new waterway cut across the Egyptian desert. The Suez Canal had opened, joining the Mediterranean to the Red Sea, and the journey from Europe to Asia became thousands of miles shorter.

Today is International Students' Day. It remembers the students of Prague, who on this date in 1939 were attacked and arrested by the Nazis for protesting. Fifty years later, on the very same date in 1989, students marched through Prague again. This time their peaceful protest grew into the Velvet Revolution, and communism in Czechoslovakia fell without a shot.

In 1558, a young woman named Elizabeth became Queen of England, and a golden age began.

And in 1970, a Soviet robot called Lunokhod 1 rolled off its lander onto the Moon, the first wheeled vehicle to explore another world.

Born on this day in 1942 was Martin Scorsese, one of the great storytellers of cinema.

11-18.script:
On the eighteenth of November in 1928, audiences in New York watched a little cartoon mouse whistle as he steered a riverboat. Steamboat Willie was one of the first cartoons with synchronised sound, and Mickey Mouse became a star.

Before that day in 1883, nearly every town in America kept its own time by the Sun, and the railways were in a muddle. At noon on the eighteenth of November, the railroads switched to a handful of standard time zones, and clocks across the continent fell into step.

In 1918, Latvia declared its independence, and today Latvians celebrate with candles and flags.

In 1626, Pope Urban the Eighth consecrated the new Saint Peter's Basilica in Rome, after more than a century of building.

Born on this day in 1787 was Louis Daguerre, whose silvered plates gave us some of the first photographs, and in 1923, Alan Shepard, the first American in space, who would one day hit golf balls on the Moon.

births.text: Louis Daguerre, French pioneer of photography
W. S. Gilbert, English librettist (Gilbert and Sullivan)
Alec Issigonis, British designer of the Mini

facts.text: Mickey Mouse's birthday is celebrated on 18 November, the day Steamboat Willie premiered.

11-19.script:
On the nineteenth of November in 1863, at a new cemetery in Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, Abraham Lincoln rose and spoke for barely two minutes. Fourscore and seven years ago, he began. His few words, about a nation conceived in liberty and a government of the people, by the people, for the people, became among the most famous ever spoken.

Born on this day in 1828 was Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi, the warrior queen who rode into battle in 1857. And in 1917, Indira Gandhi was born, who would become India's first woman Prime Minister.

In 1942, the Soviet army launched Operation Uranus, encircling the German forces at Stalingrad. The tide of the Second World War began to turn.

In 1969, Apollo 12 landed on the Moon, and Pete Conrad, a short man, joked as he stepped down: that may have been a small one for Neil, but it's a long one for me.

And in 1977, Egypt's President Sadat flew to Jerusalem, the first Arab leader to visit Israel, carrying a message of peace.

events.text: Christopher Columbus lands on the island of Puerto Rico.
The mysterious prisoner known as the Man in the Iron Mask dies in the Bastille.
Abraham Lincoln delivers the Gettysburg Address.
Goldwyn Pictures is founded.
The Soviet Operation Uranus begins to encircle German forces at Stalingrad.
Ford stops making the Edsel, one of the most famous flops in car history.
Apollo 12 lands on the Moon's Ocean of Storms.
Anwar Sadat becomes the first Arab leader to visit Israel.
Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev meet for the first time, in Geneva.
The first UK National Lottery draw is held.
China launches Shenzhou 1, its first spacecraft of the program.

births.text: Indira Gandhi, Prime Minister of India

facts.text: The Gettysburg Address is only about 270 words long, and took Lincoln around two minutes to deliver.

11-20.script:
Today is World Children's Day. On the twentieth of November in 1989, the United Nations adopted the Convention on the Rights of the Child, promising every child the right to grow up safe, healthy, and heard. It has been accepted by almost every nation on Earth.

On this same date in 1945, in the courthouse at Nuremberg, the leaders of Nazi Germany went on trial before the world, and the idea that even rulers must answer for their crimes was born.

In 1910, Mexico rose in revolution, and the country still celebrates today.

In 1947, Princess Elizabeth married Philip Mountbatten at Westminster Abbey, a bright moment in a grey, post-war Britain.

And in 1998, a Russian rocket carried a module called Zarya into orbit. It was the very first piece of the International Space Station.

Born on this day in 1889 was Edwin Hubble, who discovered that the universe is expanding.

events.text: A sperm whale rams and sinks the whaleship Essex, inspiring Moby-Dick.
Pierre Lallement receives a U.S. patent for a pedal-driven bicycle.
The Mexican Revolution begins.
The Battle of Cambrai begins, with hundreds of British tanks.
The Nuremberg trials of Nazi leaders begin.
Princess Elizabeth marries Philip Mountbatten in Westminster Abbey.
Microsoft releases Windows 1.0.
The UN adopts the Convention on the Rights of the Child.
Fire badly damages Windsor Castle.
Zarya, the first module of the International Space Station, is launched.

births.text: Tipu Sultan, ruler of the Kingdom of Mysore

facts.text: World Children's Day falls on the date the UN adopted both the Declaration (1959) and the Convention (1989) on the Rights of the Child.

11-21.script:
On the twenty-first of November in 1783, in the garden of a château near Paris, two men climbed into the basket of a great blue and gold balloon built by the Montgolfier brothers. It rose into the sky and drifted across the city for about twenty-five minutes. For the first time, people had flown free.

On this day in 1877, Thomas Edison announced his new invention, a machine that could record sound and play it back. The first words he recorded were a nursery rhyme: Mary had a little lamb.

In 1953, scientists revealed that the famous Piltdown Man, supposedly an ancient human, had been a hoax all along, made from a human skull and an ape's jaw.

In 1995, at an airbase in Dayton, Ohio, leaders agreed to end the war in Bosnia.

Today is World Hello Day, and World Television Day. Born on this day in 1694 was Voltaire, who loved freedom of thought, and in 1965, Björk, Iceland's unforgettable voice.

events.text: The first free flight by people takes place, in a Montgolfier hot-air balloon over Paris.
Thomas Edison announces his phonograph.
The hospital ship HMHS Britannic, sister of the Titanic, sinks in the Aegean Sea.
Rebecca Latimer Felton is sworn in as the first woman in the U.S. Senate.
Scientists expose the Piltdown Man fossil as a hoax.
China declares a ceasefire in the Sino-Indian War.
The Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge opens in New York.
Millions tune in to the TV show Dallas to find out "Who shot J.R.?"
The Dayton Agreement is reached, ending the Bosnian War.
Protests begin in Kyiv's Independence Square, starting the Euromaidan.

facts.text: World Hello Day began in 1973 after the Yom Kippur War, inviting everyone to greet ten people as a gesture for peace.

11-22.script:
On the twenty-second of November in 1963, President John F. Kennedy rode through the streets of Dallas in an open car, waving to cheering crowds. Shots rang out, and within the hour the young president was dead. People around the world would always remember where they were when they heard the news.

On that same day, two great writers also died: C. S. Lewis, who gave us Narnia, and Aldous Huxley, who imagined a Brave New World.

But the twenty-second of November has gentler memories too. In 1995, a cowboy doll named Woody and a space ranger named Buzz Lightyear came to life in Toy Story, the first feature film made entirely by computer.

In 1928, Ravel's hypnotic Boléro was heard for the first time in Paris.

In 1943, Lebanon gained its independence. And born on this day in 1890 was Charles de Gaulle, who would lead the Free French through the darkest days of war.

events.text: Vasco da Gama's fleet rounds the Cape of Good Hope on its way to India.
The pirate Blackbeard is killed in battle off North Carolina.
Maurice Ravel's Boléro premieres in Paris.
Lebanon gains independence from France.
President John F. Kennedy is assassinated in Dallas.

Toy Story, the first entirely computer-animated feature film, is released.
Angela Merkel becomes Germany's first female Chancellor.
Microsoft's Xbox 360 games console goes on sale.

births.text: André Gide, French author and Nobel laureate
Charles de Gaulle, President of France
Billie Jean King, American tennis player

deaths.text: C. S. Lewis, British author of the Narnia books

facts.text: Boléro repeats a single melody again and again for about 15 minutes, growing louder all the way.
Toy Story took about four years to make, with every frame drawn by computer.

11-23.script:
On the twenty-third of November in 1963, a strange blue police box appeared on British television. Inside, it was far bigger than outside, and it belonged to a mysterious traveller called the Doctor. Doctor Who had begun its journey through time and space, a journey that still continues.

In 1889, in a saloon in San Francisco, people dropped a nickel into a machine and listened through tubes as it played a recording. It was one of the first jukeboxes.

In 1924, newspapers reported an astonishing discovery by the astronomer Edwin Hubble. The faint smudge called Andromeda was not a cloud inside our galaxy, but another galaxy altogether, unimaginably far away. The universe had suddenly become much, much larger.

In 1936, the first issue of Life magazine was published, and photographs began to tell the news.

In Japan, today is Labour Thanksgiving Day, a day to thank one another for our work.

events.text: One of the first jukeboxes goes into service in a San Francisco saloon.
Edwin Hubble's discovery that Andromeda is a separate galaxy is reported.
The first issue of Life magazine is published.
Romania joins the Axis powers.
The Battle of Tarawa ends in the Pacific.

IBM shows the Simon, often called the first smartphone.
Ellen Johnson Sirleaf is confirmed as Liberia's president, Africa's first elected female head of state.

births.text: Franklin Pierce, 14th President of the United States
Sathya Sai Baba, Indian spiritual teacher

facts.text: Labour Thanksgiving Day grew from Niiname-sai, an ancient harvest festival in which the emperor offers the new rice to the gods.
Doctor Who's first episode was overshadowed by news of Kennedy's assassination, so the BBC showed it again the following week.

11-24.script:
On the twenty-fourth of November in 1859, a quiet naturalist named Charles Darwin published a book called On the Origin of Species. Every copy sold out on the first day. His idea that all living things change slowly over time, shaped by nature, would transform how we understand life itself. Today some celebrate it as Evolution Day.

Fittingly, on this same date in 1974, in the dusty hills of Ethiopia, scientists found the bones of one of our ancient ancestors. That night, a Beatles song was playing in their camp, and they named her Lucy.

In 1642, the Dutch explorer Abel Tasman sighted the coast of an island that would one day bear his name: Tasmania.

And in 1971, a man calling himself Dan Cooper hijacked a plane, collected a ransom, and leapt out into the night sky with a parachute. He was never seen again.

In Assam, today is Lachit Divas, honouring the general Lachit Borphukan. A day for the long story of life.

events.text: Abel Tasman sights the island later named Tasmania.
Charles Darwin publishes On the Origin of Species.
Joseph Glidden patents barbed wire, which changes farming on the American plains.
Irish writer and nationalist Erskine Childers is executed during the Irish Civil War.

Freddie Mercury of Queen dies in London, a day after announcing he had AIDS.

births.text: Zachary Taylor, 12th President of the United States
Dale Carnegie, American writer (How to Win Friends and Influence People)

facts.text: Lucy was named after the Beatles song "Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds", which was playing at the camp the night she was found.

names: International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women
11-25.script:
Today the world stands against violence towards women. The date was chosen to remember the Mirabal sisters, three brave women in the Dominican Republic who opposed a dictator and were killed on the twenty-fifth of November, 1960. They are remembered as the Butterflies.

On this day in 1915, in Berlin, Albert Einstein presented the final equations of his theory of general relativity. Space and time, he showed, bend and curve around everything that has mass. It is how we understand gravity to this day.

In 1952, a murder mystery by Agatha Christie opened in London. The Mousetrap has been playing almost ever since, the longest-running play in the world.

In 1984, dozens of British musicians gathered in a studio to record Do They Know It's Christmas, raising money for famine relief in Ethiopia.

In 1975, Suriname became independent. And born on this day in 1835 was Andrew Carnegie, who gave away most of his fortune to build libraries.

events.text: The last British troops leave New York City.
Albert Einstein presents the field equations of general relativity.
The de Havilland Mosquito, a fast warplane built mostly of wood, makes its first flight.
Agatha Christie's The Mousetrap opens in London, beginning the world's longest-running play.
Hungary beat England 6–3 at Wembley, England's first home defeat by a team from outside the British Isles.

USS Enterprise, the first nuclear-powered aircraft carrier, enters service.

Band Aid records "Do They Know It's Christmas?".

births.text: Andrew Carnegie, Scottish-American industrialist and philanthropist
John F. Kennedy Jr., American lawyer and publisher

facts.text: The day against violence towards women honours the Mirabal sisters, remembered as "Las Mariposas" — the Butterflies.

11-26.script:
On the twenty-sixth of November in 1949, India's Constituent Assembly adopted the Constitution, the longest written constitution of any nation, guided by Dr. B. R. Ambedkar. It promised justice, liberty, equality and fraternity to every citizen. Today India celebrates Constitution Day.

It is also National Milk Day, the birthday in 1921 of Verghese Kurien, who helped turn India into the world's largest producer of milk.

On this day in 1922, in the Valley of the Kings, Howard Carter made a small hole in a sealed doorway and held up a candle. Lord Carnarvon asked if he could see anything. Yes, Carter replied, wonderful things.

In 1942, the film Casablanca premiered in New York. Here's looking at you, kid.

And in 2018, the InSight lander touched down on Mars to listen to the heartbeat of the red planet.

The day also carries grief. In 2008, terrorists attacked Mumbai, and the city showed the world its courage.

events.text: The United States celebrates its first national Thanksgiving, proclaimed by George Washington.
The first national Thanksgiving Day, proclaimed by Lincoln, is celebrated in the U.S.
Lewis Carroll's Alice's Adventures in Wonderland is published.
Howard Carter first looks into Tutankhamun's tomb and sees "wonderful things".
The United States hands Japan the Hull note, days before the attack on Pearl Harbor.

NASA's InSight lander touches down on Mars.

births.text: John Harvard, English benefactor of Harvard University
Verghese Kurien, father of India's White Revolution
Charles M. Schulz, American cartoonist of Peanuts

facts.text: India's Constitution, adopted on this day, is the longest written national constitution in the world.

11-27.script:
On the twenty-seventh of November in 1895, in Paris, the inventor Alfred Nobel signed his last will. He left most of his fortune to create prizes for those who had brought the greatest benefit to humankind, in physics, chemistry, medicine, literature, and peace. The Nobel Prizes were born from a single sheet of paper.

Centuries earlier, in 1095, Pope Urban the Second stood before a crowd at Clermont in France and called for a crusade to the Holy Land.

In 1924, giant balloons and marching bands paraded through New York for the first Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade.

In 1971, the Soviet probe Mars 2 crashed onto the red planet, the first human-made object ever to reach its surface.

And in 1978, Harvey Milk, one of the first openly gay elected officials in America, was killed in San Francisco. Thousands marched that night with candles.

Born on this day were Anders Celsius in 1701, who gave us his temperature scale, Bruce Lee in 1940, and Jimi Hendrix in 1942.

events.text: Pope Urban II calls for the First Crusade at the Council of Clermont.
The Great Storm batters southern England, wrecking ships and homes.
Alfred Nobel signs his will, creating the Nobel Prizes.

Surgeons in France perform the first partial face transplant.

births.text: Chaim Weizmann, first President of Israel
Bruce Lee, martial artist and actor

facts.text: Anders Celsius, born today, first designed his scale with water boiling at 0 and freezing at 100 — the reverse of today's.
Alfred Nobel's will left most of his fortune to the prizes, to the surprise of his family.
Jimi Hendrix, born today, played a right-handed guitar turned upside down.

11-28.script:
On the twenty-eighth of November in 1520, after weeks of struggling through a stormy strait at the tip of South America, Ferdinand Magellan's ships sailed out into a vast, calm ocean. Grateful for its peaceful waters, he called it the Pacific.

On this day in 1893, women in New Zealand went to the polls in a national election for the very first time, the first country in the world where women could do so.

In 1912, Albania declared its independence, and today Albanians celebrate with music and red-and-black flags. Mauritania too became independent on this date in 1960.

In 1943, Churchill, Roosevelt and Stalin met together for the first time, in Tehran, to plan the end of the war.

In 1964, NASA launched Mariner 4, which would send back the first close-up pictures of Mars.

Born on this day in 1757 was William Blake, the poet who saw a world in a grain of sand.

events.text: Ferdinand Magellan's ships enter the ocean he names the Pacific.
The Royal Society, one of the world's oldest scientific academies, is founded in London.
Women vote in a New Zealand general election for the first time.
Albania declares its independence from the Ottoman Empire.

names: International Day of Solidarity with the Palestinian People
11-29.script:
On the twenty-ninth of November in 1929, the explorer Richard Byrd and his crew flew over the South Pole for the first time, dropping a small flag weighted with a stone from a friend's grave.

In 1961, a chimpanzee named Enos orbited the Earth twice aboard a Mercury capsule, paving the way for America's first astronaut to orbit, just a few months later.

In 1899, a group of young football lovers in Barcelona founded a club. FC Barcelona would become one of the most famous teams in the world.

In 1947, the United Nations voted to divide Palestine into two states. Today the world marks a day of solidarity with the Palestinian people.

In 1972, a simple game appeared in a California bar: two paddles and a bouncing ball. Pong had arrived, and the video game industry was born.

Born on this day in 1832 was Louisa May Alcott, who wrote Little Women, and in 1898, C. S. Lewis, who opened the wardrobe to Narnia.

events.text: The Times of London is printed on a steam-powered press for the first time.
The November Uprising against Russian rule begins in Poland.
FC Barcelona is founded.
Richard Byrd's expedition makes the first flight over the South Pole.
Surgeons at Johns Hopkins perform the first "blue baby" heart operation.
Yugoslavia is proclaimed a federal people's republic.
The UN General Assembly votes to partition Palestine.
The chimpanzee Enos orbits the Earth aboard Mercury-Atlas 5.
President Lyndon Johnson creates the Warren Commission to investigate Kennedy's assassination.
Atari releases the arcade game Pong.

births.text: Louisa May Alcott, American author of Little Women
C. S. Lewis, British author of the Narnia books

facts.text: C. S. Lewis, born today, imagined Narnia as a land where it was "always winter and never Christmas".
Louisa May Alcott, born today, shared her birthday with her father, Bronson Alcott.

11-30.script:
Today is Saint Andrew's Day in Scotland, and fittingly, on the thirtieth of November in 1872, Scotland and England met in Glasgow for the very first international football match. After ninety minutes, the score was nil, nil.

On this day in 1954, in Alabama, a woman named Ann Hodges was napping on her sofa when a meteorite crashed through her roof and bounced off her radio onto her hip. She is the only person known to have been hit by a meteorite.

In 1936, the glittering Crystal Palace in London, built of glass and iron, burned down in a single night.

In 1982, Michael Jackson released Thriller, which became the best-selling album of all time.

Barbados became independent on this date in 1966, and in 2021, on the very same day, it became a republic.

And born on this day were three great storytellers: Jonathan Swift in 1667, Mark Twain in 1835, and Winston Churchill in 1874. In 1858, Jagadish Chandra Bose was born, who showed the world that plants respond to their surroundings, almost as if they could feel.
